articles.title: Middle East live: Oil prices extend gains as US-Iran tensions flare again
articles.body:
Middle East live: Oil prices extend gains as US-Iran tensions flare again
Oil prices rose further Tuesday as renewed military exchanges between the United States and Iran, coupled with Donald Trump’s vow to hit Tehran “hard,” fueled fears of a broader escalation after weeks of relative calm. Follow our live blog for the latest developments.
Iran's president thanks Russia for position on war, says Tehran and Moscow resist US 'unilateralism'
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian thanked Russian President Vladimir Putin on Tuesday for Moscow's position on the Iran war and resulting sanctions, and said together, Moscow and Tehran can resist what he called the US "unilateralism".
The two men spoke during a meeting in the Kyrgyz capital Bishkek.
Iran's Pezeshkian meets Putin on sidelines of Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit
Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian held talks on Tuesday with Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Kyrgyzstan, the Iranian presidency said.
"During the meeting, the latest state of bilateral relations between Iran and Russia was reviewed and the two sides discussed ways to strengthen and expand cooperation in various fields," said the presidency in a statement accompanied by images of Putin and Pezeshkian shaking hands.
Two tankers hit by 'unknown projectiles' in Hormuz, security firm reports
"Unknown projectiles" struck two oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz overnight, a Greek security firm said.
"Two crude oil tankers were struck by unknown projectiles within minutes of each other while transiting outbound through the Strait of Hormuz late on August 31," Greek maritime risk management firm Marisks said.
One of the incidents had been publicised earlier by the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency, which added that no casualties or environmental effects had been reported.
Israeli strikes on Gaza came during operation to capture Hamas figure, officials say
Heavy Israeli bombardment killed three people in Gaza City, Palestinian health officials said, in what both sides described as an Israeli-backed ground operation to seize a senior Hamas figure.
Eyewitnesses reported around a dozen strikes on Tuesday morning in western Gaza City, where the territory's civil defence agency said three people were killed, including two children and a woman.
Speaking on the Israeli side of the Gaza border, Defence Minister Israel Katz announced that "a senior Hamas terrorist was arrested" without naming the person or giving further details.
Security sources in Gaza gave a different account, with one telling AFP the Israeli mission against a prominent Hamas figure was thwarted and that special forces withdrew "on motorcycles under Israeli cover".
The forces included an Israeli-allied militia inside Gaza.
Ismail al-Thawabta, head of Hamas's media office in Gaza, said an Israeli special forces operation was "exposed during the mission", prompting heavy air strikes in the area that he alleged also killed members of the special forces.
Americas continue to capture greater market share of global oil production
From Canada to Argentina, oil producers across the Americas have enjoyed a windfall during the Iran war by capturing market share lost by Middle Eastern exporters.
The renewed focus on energy security globally could transform this emergency response into a lasting structural change.
Oil production in the Americas has become a viable alternative to the Middle East's vast hydrocarbon resources since the outbreak of the Iran war and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz six months ago, which disrupted roughly a fifth of global oil supplies.
The shift is one of the most striking changes in the global energy landscape in decades.
Crude exports from the region, stretching from Canada in the north to Argentina in the south, have risen to a record-high average of 11.7 million barrels per day (bpd) so far in 2026, up from 10.3 million bpd in 2025, and nearly double the volume a decade ago, according to Kpler data.
The U.S. leads the pack with exports averaging 4.4 million bpd this year, followed by Brazil at 2.5 million bpd.
Inflation leaps to three-year peak at 3.3% amid rising energy costs
Eurozone inflation jumped to 3.3 percent in August, the highest level in three years, as the war in the Middle East kept pushing up energy costs, official data showed Tuesday.
Well above the European Central Bank's two-percent target, the figure from the EU's statistical office was up sharply from 2.9 percent in July and in line with forecasts by analysts for Bloomberg.
"Looking at the main components of euro area inflation, energy is expected to have the highest annual rate in August," Eurostat said, noting that energy prices were up 14.3 percent in August after rising 10.3 percent in July.
Funding cuts force UN's WFP to halve West Bank aid recipients
The United Nations' food agency warned that funding cuts were forcing it to slash the number of aid recipients in the Israeli-occupied West Bank in half, warning of dire consequences.
The World Food Programme said that from this month it would be reducing the number of people it reaches with food aid in the Palestinian territory from 400,000 to 200,000.
"This is happening as the food needs in the West Bank are more than double what they were two years ago," Shaun Hughes, the agency's representative in the Palestinian territories, told reporters.
He pointed out that food insecurity had not traditionally been a major problem in the West Bank.
But he argued that since the Gaza war began in October 2023, "intensified settler violence, prolonged and escalating Israeli military operations, severe movement restrictions, demolitions and widespread displacement in the West Bank have eroded Palestinian livelihoods and contributed to increased food insecurity".
The WFP said that its latest quarterly food security analysis found that 76 percent of households in the West Bank had experienced a significant decline in income, with many families forced to sell assets and reduce the number and quality of their meals to survive.
Israeli forces kills four people, including three children, in Gaza, medics say
Israel's military killed at least four people, including three children, with gunfire and air strikes in the Gaza Strip, health officials said.
Witnesses said Israeli warplanes fired at least 12 missiles near the Katiba area in the west of Gaza City, an area crowded with displaced families.
At least three people – two children and a woman – were killed and several others wounded in the unusually heavy bombardment, medics said. Two vehicles were hit and reduced to twisted wreckage.
In a statement on Tuesday, the Israeli military said it struck several targets in the Gaza Strip in order to remove threats to Israeli security forces.
In a separate incident, medics said Israeli forces operating east of Deir Al-Balah in central Gaza shot dead a girl, Israa Al-Hissi, and wounded two other people.
Israeli military says it struck several targets in Gaza
The Israeli military said it struck several targets in the Gaza Strip, claiming the strikes were aimed at removing threats to its forces.
Tanker hit by three 'unknown projectiles' in Hormuz, maritime agency reports
Three "unknown projectiles" struck a tanker in the Strait of Hormuz overnight, a British maritime agency said Tuesday following a fresh flare-up in the US-Iran war.
"A tanker has reported being struck by 3 unknown projectiles whilst completing an outbound transit of the Strait of Hormuz," the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations said on X early Tuesday.
The incident occurred 17 nautical miles (31 kilometres) east of the Oman city of Khasab, it added.
No casualties or environmental impact were reported, the agency said.
Maritime security company Vanguard Tech later identified the ship as the Liberia-flagged Senegal Prosperity.
"The rockets impacted the vessel's port side, engine room and ballast tank, resulting in a loss of communications," Vanguard said, adding that the crew were safe.
Iran says it has enough foreign currency despite US sanctions
Iran has sufficient foreign currency reserves despite US sanctions, Central Bank Governor Abdolnaser Hemmati said, after US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent accused Tehran of lashing out because it was losing the economic war.
The central bank was ready to inject up to $2 billion into the foreign exchange market to calm recent volatility, Hemmati said, according to the semi-official Tasnim news agency.
“I am telling the President of the United States: Iran has (foreign) currency and it has enough,” he added.
Hemmati said the central bank was continuing to collect foreign currency receivables and had domestic reserves as well as other resources, though he added details of those could not be disclosed.
"I tell the people with complete honesty that economic conditions and livelihood management have become difficult, but collapse has never happened and will never happen. These claims are just psychological warfare and the dust will settle soon," Hemmati said.
Iran’s currency plunged to a record low in August, crossing the threshold of 2 million rials to the US dollar, while annual inflation reached 66 percent in July.
Iran's President Pezeshkian says Tehran will reciprocate if US honours interim deal commitments
Iran will immediately reciprocate if the US returns to its commitments under an interim deal signed in June, President Masoud Pezeshkian said at the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation Summit in Bishkek, the Iranian Student News Agency reported.
Strait of Hormuz shipping remains sharply below normal levels
Ship traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remained subdued on Monday, with around five vessels making the passage compared with a 10-day average of about 14, preliminary tracking data showed. No liquid tankers transited the key waterway, although the figures exclude vessels sailing with their transponders switched off.
Oil prices extend gains as US-Iran tensions flare again
Oil prices extended their gains Tuesday after a fresh exchange of strikes between the United States and Iran raised fears of renewed escalation. Washington struck Iranian rocket launchers on the island of Larak on Sunday, prompting Tehran to target US forces in Jordan and the United Arab Emirates. US President Donald Trump vowed the US would respond and “hit them hard", despite his administration’s recent shift toward an economic pressure campaign.
The renewed tensions come after six months of war, with Iran still blocking the Strait of Hormuz and the US maintaining a blockade of Iranian ports. Higher oil prices are adding to inflation concerns and expectations of higher interest rates, weighing on global stock markets. Trump is due to meet US oil refining executives Tuesday as soaring gasoline prices become a political liability ahead of November’s midterm elections.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP, AP and Reuters)

articles.title: Trump threatens to ‘hit Iran hard’ after new flare-up
articles.body:
Trump threatens to ‘hit Iran hard’ after new flare-up
US President Donald Trump has vowed to “hit Iran hard” following Tehran’s retaliatory strikes on US military installations in Jordan, raising the prospect of another round of escalation after a month-long lull in direct fighting.
Iran fired ballistic missiles and drones at US military positions after US forces struck Larak Island in the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said its attack targeted the King Hussein and Al-Azraq air bases in Jordan in retaliation for the US strike, which Tehran said killed two Iranian soldiers and a civilian and injured several others.
“There will be a response,” Trump told Fox News reporter Trey Yingst by phone on Monday. “We’re going to hit them hard.”
Jordan said its air defenses intercepted eight missiles that entered its airspace, with no damage officially reported on the ground. Trump claimed that US forces allowed one incoming missile to pass through their defenses after determining that it was not going to hit anything “significant.”
Despite threatening further military action, Trump suggested that negotiations remain possible. “They want to meet so badly,” he told Fox. “The sanctions are kicking in really strongly.”
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Tehran is “not looking for war” but would deliver a “decisive response” to further attacks.
Trump and senior US officials were already considering a plan for periodic strikes on Iranian military capabilities around the Strait of Hormuz before the latest exchange, Axios reported, citing three US officials.
The proposal, developed by US Central Command and backed by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, would target Iranian radar, air defenses, and anti-ship missile capabilities as they are rebuilt. One US official described the proposed approach as an effort to “mow the lawn.”
The renewed military threats come after the Trump administration shifted much of its pressure campaign toward economic measures, launching an “economic onslaught” against Iran’s trade partners under Operation Economic Outcast.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Sunday that Washington plans to roll out new secondary sanctions every week against foreign banks and companies that continue doing business with Iran, warning allies and rivals alike that they could be cut off from the US financial system.
“You’re either with us or you’re with the Iranians,” Bessent said, adding that Washington is prepared to use “financial violence if we have to.”

articles.title: Russia Has Quintupled Use of Jet-Powered Drones Against Ukraine, According to Yurii Ihnat
articles.body:
In July 2026, Russia increased its use of jet-powered UAVs against Ukraine fivefold compared with June.
On August 31, Yurii Ihnat, the Head of the Communications Department of the Air Force Command of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, stated this during a telethon, Interfax-Ukraine reports.
According to him, over the past four days, Ukrainian forces have recorded more than 1,500 drones, about 800 of which were jet-powered.
The overall effectiveness of Ukraine’s air defense was about 90%, but jet-powered UAVs were intercepted less frequently.
Ihnat noted that Russia began actively using jet-powered UAVs in July.
Over the course of a month, their number increased fivefold compared with June. Russian forces have also stepped up their use of Banderol-type UAVs, which combine the features of a drone and a missile.
According to the Air Force spokesperson, the new jet-powered UAVs are significantly harder to intercept due to their high speed.
Some of these vehicles can reach speeds of around 600 km/h, while Ukrainian interceptor drones currently reach approximately 300 km/h and physically cannot catch up with such targets.
Another challenge is the altitude at which jet-powered UAVs fly — around 5 km.
As a result, they operate beyond the effective engagement range of mobile fire teams and portable SAM systems.
Yurii Ihnat attributes the increased use of jet-powered UAVs to the high effectiveness of Ukrainian air defense against Shahed drones. According to him, Russia is attempting to shift to more complex and faster attack systems that require a wider range of interception capabilities.
This is also confirmed by the Russian military’s increased use of the S8000 Banderol cruise missile. Russia is currently producing the missile at a rate of approximately 80 units per month.
Experts classify the S8000 Bandrol as a small cruise missile or a jet-powered loitering munition that combines the features of a kamikaze drone and a missile. Its designers developed it with a focus on minimizing cost and simplifying production while retaining sufficient capabilities to strike targets at operational depth.
We also recommend reading this article on Militarnyi — “S8000 ‘Banderol’: A New Russian Missile for Strikes Against Ukraine.”
In appearance and aerodynamic configuration, the weapon resembles a miniature cruise missile, with a design that incorporates low-observability requirements. The fuselage is approximately 5 meters long, with a body diameter of around 30 centimeters. The missile features folding wings and stabilizers with a span of about 2.2 meters. This allows it to be transported in a folded configuration or mounted on the external pylons of aircraft carriers.
The small body diameter and use of composite materials reduce the target’s radar cross section. This makes it more difficult for radar stations to detect the missile, particularly when it flies at extremely low altitudes, where it can use the terrain for concealment.

articles.title: Trump mulls resuming Iran war after first strikes in weeks
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Trump mulls resuming Iran war after first exchange of fire in weeks
US President Donald Trump and his senior aides are considering resuming the war on Iran in a bid to prevent it from attacking ships in the Strait of Hormuz , three US officials told Axios.
The report came several hours after Trump threatened to hit Iran "hard" after the two foes traded fire for the first time in over a month.
After six months of war, the foes remain at an impasse, with Iran keeping the strategic Strait of Hormuz closed and the US persisting with a naval counter-blockade of Iran.
According to Axios, the plan was drawn up US Central Command (CENTCOM) and is backed by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. It would stop short of full-scale war in favour of limited strikes targeting Iranian missile and radar sites.
One official described the floated operation as "mowing the lawn", a popular term among Israeli military officials to describe the periodic bombing of Gaza.
"The President retains all options at his disposal. The Iranians want to make a deal, but they are always a day late and a dollar short," a White House official told the news outlet.
Late Sunday, the United States said it had carried out strikes on an Iranian island in the Strait of Hormuz, with Tehran quickly retaliating by attacking US military targets in the Middle East.
The exchange raised fears of a return to major hostilities, with the US president vowing to respond.
"We're going to hit them hard," Trump said, according to a Fox News reporter who spoke to him briefly. "There will be a response."
The United States said it attacked Iranian rocket launchers on the island of Larak to prevent Tehran planting mines in the key shipping lane.
Iran responded by with missile and drone attacks aimed at Jordan and the United Arab Emirates, saying they targeted US forces there, but President Masoud Pezeshkian later on Monday called for dialogue.
"We continue to strive for a path of agreement and understanding, and we believe that continuing the war is neither in our interest, nor in the interest of the region," he said at a summit in Kyrgyzstan, adding "the solution to the existing problems is dialogue and cooperation".
State media reported that two people were killed in the US attack on Larak, with several others wounded.
Iran's powerful Revolutionary Guards, the ideological arm of its military, said the ballistic missile attack on two US air bases in Jordan caused "heavy damage".
Jordan's army said it had intercepted eight missiles, without stating their origin. Trump also told Fox that all the missiles fired at US forces had been shot down, except for one that was determined not to pose a threat.
Iran also said it targeted US personnel at an air base in the UAE and shot down an American drone over Hormuz.
Abu Dhabi said it intercepted a drone over the country's waters, but dismissed claims that Al Minhad Air Base had been targeted as "baseless".
The exchange of fire came after weeks of relative calm, with the Trump administration recently pivoting to "economic warfare".
Earlier on Monday, Trump had called Iran "a Failed Nation", saying on social media that its military was decimated, its finances were crumbling "and their leadership is in total disarray and incapable of properly representing the country".
Hormuz flashpoint
The two sides are still vying for control of the Strait of Hormuz, with Tehran having blocked the passage of commercial ships since the war began, attacking vessels that seek to cross.
One-fifth of the world's oil passed through the strait before the war, which was triggered by a surprise wave of US and Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28.
Despite traffic remaining throttled six months on, Trump has claimed the US navy has "total control" of the strait and has even called it US territory, with Washington last week announcing it had completed clearing explosives from the waterway.
Iran, however, insists it is in charge of the sealane. The Revolutionary Guards said Monday a "rogue" oil tanker caught fire near the strait after it hit two mines while attempting to transit an "illegal route".
The US military called the claim "disinformation", saying: "No ships have hit mines in the Strait of Hormuz."
Mediators have tried for months to broker an end to the war, but an earlier truce and memorandum of understanding fell apart.
Sporadic attacks resumed, but ultimately tapered off, with the US last striking Iran on 29 July, after having attacked Iran for 13 consecutive nights earlier that month.
With diplomacy stalled, Iran's foreign minister on Monday accused Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of tricking Washington into going to war.
"In Hebrew, Netanyahu openly crows that he suckered the US administration into a war on Iran on behalf of Israel," Abbas Araghchi wrote on X. "In English, he praises POTUS' leadership. Serpent."
(AFP and TNA staff)

articles.title: Russia attacked with ballistic and "Zircon" missiles; some of missiles and 187 of 218 drones neutralized

Russia attacked with ballistic and "Zircon" missiles; some of missiles and 187 of 218 drones neutralized
Kyiv • UNN
Russia launched 218 drones and missiles at Ukraine overnight, including ballistic missiles and "Zircon" missiles. Air defenses shot down or suppressed 199 targets.
Russia launched ballistic missiles, Zircon and other missiles, Banderoľ munitions, and 218 drones at Ukraine overnight; five ballistic missiles, two Banderoľ munitions, five Kalibr missiles, and 187 unmanned aerial vehicles were shot down or suppressed, while some missiles failed to reach their targets, the Ukrainian Air Force reported on Tuesday, UNN writes.
Details
According to the Ukrainian Air Force, during the night of September 1 (from 18:00 on August 31), the enemy attacked with:
-  Iskander-M/KN-23/S-400 ballistic missiles and Zircon anti-ship missiles from Russia’s Bryansk, Kursk, Voronezh, and Rostov regions; 
-  sea-launched Kalibr cruise missiles from Novorossiysk; 
-  Kh-31P anti-radiation missiles from the airspace over the Black Sea; 
-  S8000 Banderoľ munitions from Russia’s Bryansk region and from over the Sea of Azov; 
-  218 Shahed-type attack UAVs (about one-third of them jet-powered) and Parodya-type decoy drones from the following directions: Kursk, Millerovo, Orel, Primorsko-Akhtarsk – Russia, the temporarily occupied territory of Donetsk region, and Hvardiiske – the temporarily occupied territory of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea. 
"The main directions of the attack were Odesa region and Kyiv region," the statement said.
The air attack was repelled by aviation, surface-to-air missile forces, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of Ukraine’s Defense Forces.
According to preliminary data, as of 08:30, air defenses had shot down/suppressed 199 targets: five Iskander-M/KN-23/S-400 ballistic missiles; two S8000 Banderoľ munitions; five Kalibr cruise missiles; and 187 enemy Shahed-type UAVs, Gerbera drones, and drones of other types. Hits by enemy missiles and attack UAVs were recorded at 28 locations, as well as the falling of downed targets (debris) at 10 locations. In addition, some enemy missiles failed to reach their targets; information regarding their locations is being clarified. Unfortunately, there were deaths and injuries as a result of the Russian attack; we express our condolences to the families and loved ones...
The attack is ongoing; more than ten enemy UAVs are in the airspace.

articles.title: Ukrainian pilot details fight against jet-powered Shaheds
articles.body:
- A Ukrainian fighter pilot told Waypoint that jet-powered Shahed drones remain a difficult but viable target for crewed fighter jets despite the cost.
- He said Ukraine's main constraint is funding and procedural delays, not a failure of its layered air defense system.
A Ukrainian fighter pilot who runs the social media channel “Sonyashnyk” told the outlet Waypoint that jet-powered Shahed drones remain difficult to stop even as Ukraine’s air defense system continues to evolve, arguing that focus on the small number of drones that get through overlooks the far larger number destroyed before they reach populated areas.
The pilot, whose name was not disclosed, was asked where Ukraine’s air defense system fails most against jet-powered Shahed drones. He said no country’s air defense system could withstand the volume of daily Russian strikes, and pushed back on the idea that Ukraine’s system is failing.
“The amount of resources the enemy uses daily is colossal. Civilians focus on the number of targets that got through some echelon of our defense, but forget that downing enemy targets starts back over the swamps,” the pilot said.
He said Russia has adapted its tactics over the course of the war after realizing it could not overwhelm Ukraine’s defenses carelessly, now preparing major strikes with extensive resources and support from what he called allied “tyrants.” He said Russia has found gaps Ukraine currently lacks the means to close, including exploiting national borders and launching mass strikes during periods of worsening weather.
“In my opinion, our Achilles heel is funding, both from partners and locally. Many important initiatives and ideas have to pass through a hundred procedural councils before anyone hears them,” the pilot said. “As for allies, the world is still moving too slowly into World War III. That’s where the shortage of ammunition and other resources comes from.”
Asked whether it still makes sense to send crewed fighter jets after jet-powered Shaheds, given the cost involved, the pilot said the mission remains within a fighter jet’s core role of air dominance and integrated air defense work.
“From a fighter’s perspective it makes sense, because that’s literally our specialty: air dominance and working within the air defense system,” the pilot said. He said the older Geran-1 and Geran-2 drones had been a persistent nuisance for a period, but described the jet-powered Shahed as a comparatively good target given its flight characteristics.
“Financially it’s painful, but that’s our purpose,” he said. “In a single sortie even an old MiG can take out a dozen or so. You have to understand that since there aren’t many other options, you end up relying on skill and experience.” He added that some enemy targets fly at altitudes where cheaper interceptors simply cannot reach them or arrive in time.
Asked for two or three real priorities for countering jet-powered Shaheds systematically rather than case by case, the pilot said destroying the launch sites themselves is not realistic, since Russia can rebuild or relocate them, including launching from mobile platforms.
“Of course we need to conduct operations on enemy territory, hunt launch sites and logistics, factories and workshops,” he said. “But I also think that if all our forces are directed toward that alone, the enemy will simply move faster to operate from underground.” He said the more logical approach is parallel work: building out a layered, unified air defense system, even if unified only by sector or “line,” while continuously pressuring the enemy’s capabilities.
“If we’re given a sufficient quantity of interception means and expand the authority of commanders and leaders on the ground, then with competent coordination everything will be fine,” he said. He pointed to a shift he said Ukrainians witnessed roughly six months earlier, when, with sufficient interception resources available, only a pair of drones out of hundreds launched toward Kyiv managed to get through.

articles.title: Russian missile and drone attack on Kyiv kills at least eight
articles.body:
Russian missile and drone attack on Kyiv kills at least eight
A massive Russian missile and drone attack on Kyiv and its surrounding region killed at least eight people and wounded more than a dozen overnight, Ukrainian officials said Tuesday, as children prepared to return to school amid heightened fears of further strikes.
A "massive" Russian missile and drone attack on Kyiv and its surrounding areas killed at least eight and wounded more than a dozen others, Ukrainian officials said Tuesday.
The strikes came as children were set to return to school after the summer holidays, and as officials tightened security measures during fears of further Russian strikes.
"Kyiv region came under a massive attack by Russian missiles and strike drones tonight," Kyiv regional military administration chief Tymur Tkachenko said on Telegram.
AFP journalists in the capital heard around a dozen loud explosions and saw flashes in sky early Tuesday moments after the air force warned of incoming ballistic missiles.
"Sadly, 3 people were killed in the enemy attack on the capital," the city military admnistration said, adding that were reports of five wounded.
Strikes in Boryspil, east of Kyiv, damaged a business, leaving one person dead and another wounded, Tkachenko said, adding that eight more were wounded when a residential building was hit.
The Ukrainian air force had earlier warned that the threat of "ballistic weapons and other means of attack against Kyiv and the region remains in effect", and urged residents to remain in shelters.
Ukrainian children return to school on Tuesday, and the Kyiv regional military administration has warned there must be no large events in areas with a high level of risk.
Kyiv and its surrounding areas have come under sustained pressure from Russian drone attacks in recent weeks, with jet-powered drones adding to the threat and triggering as many as a dozen air-raid alerts a day.
One weekend attack on an ammunition depot killed 38 people in the capital's suburbs.
Both sides have escalated long-range strikes in recent months, targeting infrastructure such as warehouses, businesses, and oil and port facilities, as well as ships, increasing civilian casualties.
Ukraine faces a shortage of interceptor missiles, particularly US-made Patriot systems used against ballistic threats.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

articles.title: Russia attacks Ukraine with different missiles and 218 drones: 199 aerial assets destroyed

Exclusives
Military
800 jet drones in four days: Russia is now firing type Ukraine's interceptors cannot catch. Of more than 1,500 drones launched over four days, about 800 have been jet-powered.
"In intercepts, they're screaming": Russia occupied this spit to control Ukraine's ports. Military says it has now isolated 2,500-strong grouping and destroyed all its artillery. Drone strikes and remote mining have cut supply, the Ukrainian soldiers say.
Intelligence and technology
Ukrainian company builds single device that detects FPV drone, reads its video feed, and jams it. Brama has passed lab and combat testing and is now going through codification.
About $150 for airframe, about $875 for finished glider: Ukraine's BlueBird is selling its drone at every stage of assembly. Units pick the control system, camera, and electronics themselves; the bare airframe starts near $150.
International
Fired Ukrainian minister offers to help build America's drone army— for Patriot missiles in return. Mykhailo Fedorov is courting US investors for a fund that would build defense tech companies itself, not just back them.

Russia's shadow war on Europe is widening—NATO still sees no attack coming. A Polish warning, a US spy chief's Moscow trip, and an explosive drone found beside a cargo plane at a German airport all preceded the alliance's assessment.

Someone placed funeral wreaths near defense companies in Lithuania and Czechia. The head of a Lithuanian defense company called it "ordinary intimidation" by Russians.

articles.title: Zelenskyy: Russia's nighttime attack claimed lives of 12 people, including an Indian citizen

Zelenskyy: Russia's nighttime attack claimed lives of 12 people, including an Indian citizen
Kyiv • UNN
Russia attacked Kyiv and 10 regions, including with jet-powered drones and ballistic missiles. Twelve people were killed, including an Indian citizen; dozens were injured.
Russia’s nighttime attack on Ukraine using a significant number of jet-powered drones and ballistic missiles claimed the lives of 12 people, including an Indian citizen, and left dozens injured, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Tuesday, reacting to another enemy strike, UNN writes.
A total of 12 people were killed, including an Indian citizen, and dozens more were injured as a result of the attack. My condolences to everyone who has lost family and loved ones

The Kherson, Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia, Kharkiv, Chernihiv, Zhytomyr, Sumy, and Dnipropetrovsk regions also came under fire."

articles.title: Ukraine’s air defenses top EU security talks
articles.body:
EU defense ministers gathered in Ireland on Sept. 1 to discuss Ukraine’s shortage of air-defense missiles and suspected hybrid attacks across Europe as Russia stepped up its strikes on the country.
Foreign ministers are due to continue the talks on Sept. 2. The informal meetings in Wicklow are being held under Ireland’s rotating EU presidency.
Ukraine has been running low on U.S.-made interceptor missiles, limiting its ability to counter Russian attacks. Kyiv has responded with long-range strikes on Russian infrastructure.
Russian attacks were becoming “harsher and harsher,” an EU official said on condition of anonymity.
Defense ministers were expected to speak with Ukrainian Defense Minister Evgeniy Khmara. Officials said there was little immediate prospect of a large increase in interceptor deliveries beyond pressing European countries with remaining stocks and asking countries such as Japan and South Korea to contribute more.
The talks will also address what European officials describe as an increase in Russian sabotage, cyberattacks and other operations below the threshold of open conflict.
EU officials said they saw no indication that Moscow was preparing a conventional attack on the bloc in the near term but expected such operations to continue.
The issue gained attention after an explosive-laden drone was found at Leipzig/Halle Airport in Germany in August. Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Germany had increasingly “found itself in the crosshairs of hybrid attackers.”
Berlin has not formally blamed Russia for the incident, and the investigation remains underway.
The EU is also considering further sanctions against Moscow. Officials have floated plans to add about 1,600 Russian individuals and entities, largely linked to the country’s defense industry, to the bloc’s sanctions list.
Several member states have also revived calls to use more than 200 billion euros ($235 billion) in frozen Russian central bank assets to finance Ukraine. An earlier proposal stalled over opposition from Belgium, where most of the assets are held.
The EU instead agreed last year to provide Kyiv with a 90-billion-euro loan intended to cover two years. Some governments now argue that the bloc may need to revisit the frozen-assets proposal as the cost of supporting Ukraine rises.
British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband and Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha are expected to join the foreign ministers’ talks.

articles.title: America has the power to defeat Iran. Why can’t it use it?
articles.body:
America has the power to defeat Iran. Why can’t it use it?
The war against Iran, launched by the United States and Israel six months ago, was conceived as a lightning campaign against a weakened and already battered enemy.
As far as is currently known, the immediate trigger was the unrest that swept Iran in January, which appears to have convinced the Israeli and American leadership that the government in Tehran was teetering on the brink of collapse and required only a final push.
At the beginning of the campaign, Donald Trump confidently predicted that the war would last a month or six weeks, and sometimes suggested it could be over even sooner. Instead, it’s become one of the defining events of the 21st century and its long-term consequences may ultimately prove comparable to those of the September 11 attacks or Russia’s military operation in Ukraine, and perhaps even surpass them.
Among the most important consequences is the damage inflicted on the United States’ position as the principal guarantor of security for the Arab states of the Persian Gulf, a role Washington gradually assumed after the Second World War, initially alongside Britain and later largely on its own.
The war has exposed two fundamental weaknesses in that first, the United States has proved unable to protect the oil infrastructure and essential services of the Gulf monarchies from devastating attacks by a middle-ranking power such as Iran, and second, it has failed to guarantee freedom of commercial navigation in strategically important waters against attacks by Iran and its Houthi allies in Yemen.
This is important far beyond the military sphere where America’s role as the Gulf’s security guarantor, spectacularly demonstrated during Operation Desert Storm in 1990-91, became one of the foundations of the post-Cold War international order. It influenced not only the foreign policies of the Arab monarchies but their financial decisions, as they invested enormous sums in the United States partly because their relationship with Washington provided them with security.
The scale of the American commitment in 1990 illustrates how much has changed.
To defend Saudi Arabia and defeat Iraq, the United States concentrated about 540,000 troops in the region, roughly a quarter of the active-duty strength of the US armed forces at the time. Seven of the Army’s 18 active divisions and two of the Marine Corps’ three divisions participated, while six of America’s 15 aircraft carriers were deployed, along with approximately 1,600 of its 6,500 combat aircraft.
Desert Storm was ultimately an overwhelming American victory achieved at remarkably low human cost, but American planners didn’t know beforehand that casualties would be so limited. Pre-war estimates envisaged as many as 20,000 casualties, including 6,000 to 7,000 dead, but despite those projections and substantial opposition in Congress, President George H.W. Bush and his administration went ahead.
The contrast with today is amazing as the United States is no longer capable of assembling anything resembling its 1990 force in the Middle East. Around 50,000 American personnel have been deployed for the current operation against Iran, supported by approximately 300 aircraft and just over 20 warships, including two aircraft carriers.
Nor has Washington managed to mobilize its allies on anything approaching the same scale, while Britain alone contributed about 35,000 personnel to the campaign against Iraq in 1990, no American ally from outside the Middle East has made a comparable contribution to the present war.
There has therefore been a radical decline in the resources the leading Western power can mobilize to defend what it regards as vital global interests, as well as in its ability to draw upon allied military power.
Curiously, this has happened without a comparable decline in America’s share of global military expenditure, given the United States accounted for roughly 35-37% of world military spending in 1990 and around 33% in 2025. This discrepancy should encourage greater skepticism about attempts to measure military power simply by comparing defense budgets.
Yet resources are only part of the explanation as more important is Washington’s apparent inability to use effectively the formidable capabilities it still possesses.
The United States undoubtedly retains the technical capacity to inflict a crushing military defeat on Iran and overthrow its government through a sufficiently large joint military operation, even with substantially fewer forces than it deployed against Iraq in 1990, but the obstacle is the price.
Any decisive operation involving a substantial ground component would probably produce many thousands of American casualties, including hundreds, and more likely thousands, of deaths. The political system that accepted such risks in 1990 appears unwilling to accept them today.
The extraordinary effort mounted on April 5, 2026, to rescue the pilot of an F-15 shot down by Iran illustrates the problem, as the United States reportedly committed 176 aircraft to the rescue and lost three manned aircraft and two or three helicopters, representing some $300 million worth of equipment.
The determination to save individual servicemen is understandable, but a military cannot expend resources on that scale to prevent individual casualties while simultaneously fighting a major war intended to achieve decisive strategic objectives.
The same caution is visible elsewhere, seeing as American troops have been kept away from the most dangerous areas, while US warships have operated at considerable distances from the Iranian coast, reducing their effectiveness. Washington has also sought to minimize public attention to its casualties, despite their relatively small number, in marked contrast with its approach during the much more dangerous operations of the early 1990s.
Then there is the financial constraint. The 1990-91 Gulf campaign cost the US budget about $64 billion, or around $120 billion when indirect costs are included. Adjusted for inflation, that would exceed $300 billion today. By mid-July, the current operation against Iran had already cost approximately $37 billion. The total is now likely between $40 billion and $50 billion, even though the campaign has failed to produce the decisive result originally envisaged.
The lesson is therefore more complicated than the simple claim that American military power has disappeared because the United States retains enormous military and financial resources. What’s changed is its ability to concentrate those resources, mobilize allies, and accept the human and financial costs required to achieve decisive political objectives.
Desert Storm demonstrated what American military supremacy looked like at its height, but the war against Iran is revealing something very different, a superpower that can still inflict enormous damage, but increasingly struggles to convert its military superiority into the political outcomes it seeks.
This article was first published by the magazine Profile and was translated and edited by the RT team.

articles.title: Air Force spokesperson says all cruise missiles were shot down during overnight attack on Ukraine
articles.body:
Air Force spokesperson says all cruise missiles were shot down during overnight attack on Ukraine
According to Ukrinform, Yurii Ihnat, head of the Communications Department of the Ukrainian Air Force Command, said this on Ukrainian television.
"We are reporting the results of missile interceptions. There were some today. Unfortunately, not as many as we would have liked. We would like to shoot down more, but that requires more capabilities, particularly more Patriot interceptor missiles. As you can see, ballistic missiles were also intercepted today. In fact, all cruise missiles were shot down. These included Kalibr missiles, while some Banderol missiles were also hit, along with a large number of drones. The interception rate remains high, despite the fact that the enemy changed its tactics today and is using many jet-powered UAVs," Ihnat said.
He noted that many ballistic missiles failed to reach their targets.
"Today, in addition to the conventional Iskander-M ballistic missiles, the enemy is using North Korean KN-23 missiles, Zircon missiles, which attack along a ballistic trajectory and approach their targets more accurately, as well as S-400 missiles. The enemy is using a considerable number of S-400 missiles, and a large number of missiles fail to reach their targets. Therefore, information on the number of missiles launched will continue to be released selectively," Ihnat explained.
He recalled that the Ukrainian Air Force provides round-the-clock, real-time information on aerial threats.
Earlier reports said that Ukrainian air defense forces neutralized five ballistic missiles, two Banderol missiles, five Kalibr cruise missiles and 187 drones used by Russian forces to attack Ukraine from the evening of August 31.

articles.title: China сomments on Finnish President’s statement on Russia’s nuclear weapons use
articles.body:
China сomments on Finnish President’s statement on Russia’s nuclear weapons use
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said this at a media briefing in response to a question about the Finnish leader’s statement, according to Ukrinform.
“Following the meeting between Foreign Minister Wang Yi and the President of Finland [on July 5 – Ed.], we issued a press release,” Guo said in response to Ukrinform’s request to comment on Stubb’s remarks about China’s non-public position regarding Russia’s nuclear weapons.
The Chinese diplomat did not deny Stubb’s claims, merely noting that Beijing’s position on the Russia-Ukraine conflict and nuclear weapons remains unchanged.
“China’s position on the ‘Ukraine crisis’ [the official term used by China for Russia’s war against Ukraine – Ed.] and on the use of nuclear weapons is consistent and clear. We continue to call for peace talks and a political settlement of the conflict,” the foreign ministry spokesperson said.
The Chinese authorities declare adherence to a defensive nuclear doctrine and a no-first-use policy, which means that China’s nuclear arsenal would be used exclusively in retaliation for a nuclear attack against China.
The official Chinese Foreign Ministry statement on Wang Yi’s meeting with Stubb on July 5 does not mention either Russia’s war or nuclear weapons.
“The current international landscape is marked by changes and turbulence, and the world risks returning to the law of the jungle. China will continue to be an important force for peace, stability and development in today’s world,” China’s top diplomat said to the Finnish president at the time.
See also: Kuchma explains why abandoning the Budapest Memorandum would not have saved Ukraine from war
As previously reported by Ukrinform, Finnish President Alexander Stubb said that China had assured him in private talks that it would not allow Russia to use nuclear weapons.

articles.title: Poland intercepts Russian spy plane over Baltic Sea again
articles.body:
- Polish fighter jets intercepted a Russian Il-20 reconnaissance aircraft over the Baltic Sea on Monday, 30 kilometers north of Łeba.
- Poland's defense minister said the aircraft did not violate Polish airspace, in at least the third such intercept reported this year.
Polish fighter jets intercepted a Russian Il-20 reconnaissance aircraft over the Baltic Sea on Monday, roughly 30 kilometers (19 miles) north of Łeba on Poland’s coast, Polish Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Defense Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said.
“Russia has once again tested our deterrence and air defense systems,” Kosiniak-Kamysz wrote. “Before noon, 30 km north of Łeba, our fighters intercepted a Russian Il-20 reconnaissance aircraft. There was no violation of our airspace over the Baltic.”
The aircraft did not violate Polish airspace, according to the minister. Monday’s intercept was at least the third publicly reported Il-20 intercept by Polish fighters over the Baltic Sea this year, following similar incidents in March, May and July.
The Il-20, known by NATO as the “Coot-A,” is a Soviet-designed signals and electronic reconnaissance aircraft derived from the Il-18 airliner. Russia regularly flies the aircraft over the Baltic Sea to collect electronic and communications intelligence, and the flights have become a recurring trigger for NATO quick reaction alert sorties in the region.
In several previous intercepts this year, Polish officials said the Il-20 was operating without a filed flight plan and with its transponder switched off. In March, Poland’s Operational Command of the Armed Forces said one such intercept marked the aircraft’s ninth reconnaissance mission of the year in the region, describing the pattern as a sustained Russian intelligence-gathering effort rather than an isolated event.
Poland has used both MiG-29 and F-16 fighters to carry out Il-20 intercepts over the Baltic this year. The MiG-29, a Soviet-designed aircraft, remains in a shrinking quick reaction alert role as Poland phases in newer F-16 and FA-50 fighters, with some retired Polish MiG-29s transferred to Ukraine.
Kosiniak-Kamysz has previously described the Il-20 flights as deliberate provocations intended to test Polish and NATO air defense response times, radar coverage and command-and-control coordination along the alliance’s eastern flank.

articles.title: Putin refused to meet with the CIA director after his proposal to end the war in Ukraine

Putin refused to meet with the CIA director after his proposal to end the war in Ukraine
Kyiv • UNN
John Ratcliffe arrived in Moscow with a call to end the war sooner and met with Naryshkin and Bortnikov. After that, the Kremlin canceled his meeting with Putin.
Russian dictator Vladimir Putin refused to meet with the head of the United States Central Intelligence Agency, John Ratcliffe, after it became clear for what purpose he had arrived in Moscow. This was reported by Russian "media," UNN reports.
Details
According to reports, Ratcliffe arrived in Moscow with a call for the Russian leadership to reach an agreement on ending the Russian-Ukrainian war as soon as possible. The CIA director proceeded from the assumption that Russia’s military and economic situation was deteriorating and that it would be more advantageous for Moscow to reach a deal now than to wait for further weakening.
During the trip, Ratcliffe also met with the head of Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service, Sergei Naryshkin, and the head of the Federal Security Service, Alexander Bortnikov. After one of these meetings, the content of the conversation was conveyed to Putin, as a result of which the Kremlin abandoned plans for a personal meeting between the Russian president and the CIA director.
We remind you
During a secret visit to Moscow, CIA Director John Ratcliffe proposed holding a trilateral meeting between U.S. President Donald Trump, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and Russian leader Vladimir Putin.
In response, Putin’s spokesman Dmitry Peskov called reports about the proposal for a trilateral summit "information hoaxes."

articles.title: Russia Returns Nuclear-Powered Cruiser Admiral Nakhimov to Navy Service After 27 Years of Repairs
articles.body:
Russia is preparing to bring back the nuclear-powered missile cruiser Admiral Nakhimov to the Russian Navy after nearly 27 years of repairs and modernization.
Russian media outlet Novye Izvestia reported on this.
It is expected to enter service with the Russian Navy by the end of 2026, following trials.
During the modernization, the cruiser received new radar systems, an AK-192M 130 mm naval gun mount, and new missile armament.
Instead of the 20 P-700 Granit anti-ship missiles, the vessel received vertical launching systems. These allow it to deploy Kalibr, Oniks, and hypersonic Zircon missiles.
According to Russian sources, the cruiser has 176 launch cells. Of these, 80 are intended for strike missiles, while another 96 are allocated for S-400 surface-to-air missiles.
Thus, following its modernization, Admiral Nakhimov is expected to combine the capabilities of a long-range strike missile carrier and a powerful air-defense vessel.
The cruiser can also operate Ka-27 or Ka-31 helicopters. The latter are equipped with a radar system that extends the detection range for airborne and surface targets and relays information to the ship’s weapon systems.
At the same time, Admiral Nakhimov is not designed to operate entirely on its own. Given its importance and size, the cruiser will require escort ships to protect it from underwater, surface, and airborne threats.
Russia may attach particular importance to its deployment in the Arctic. After returning to service with the Russian Navy, Admiral Nakhimov could become one of the fleet’s flagship assets.
Admiral Nakhimov is the third ship of the Project 1144 Orlan. It was laid down in 1983 at the Baltic Shipyard in Leningrad, launched in 1986, and commissioned into the Soviet Navy in 1988 under the name Kalinin.
In 1992, the ship was renamed in honor of Russian Admiral Pavel Nakhimov.
Project 1144 Orlan cruisers are large nuclear-powered missile ships designed to engage major surface targets, provide air and anti-submarine defense, and perform command functions.
Admiral Nakhimov belongs to Russia’s Northern Fleet, but has spent most of its service life undergoing repairs. Modernization work began back in 1999, with the active phase starting only in 2013 at the Sevmash facility in Severodvinsk.
The modernization was initially scheduled for completion in 2018, but the deadline was repeatedly postponed — first to 2020, then to 2021, 2022, 2024, and 2025. As of 2025, the total cost of the work had exceeded RUB 200 billion.
In 2024–2025, Admiral Nakhimov went to sea for trials after undergoing extensive repairs.

articles.title: Pentagon secretly hiring military influencers in social media push – WaPo
articles.body:
Pentagon secretly hiring military influencers in social media push – WaPo
The Pentagon has secretly hired conservative military veterans with a large social media following for undisclosed government roles, The Washington Post reported on Sunday. The influencers have promoted US War Secretary Pete Hegseth’s views while attacking critics of the Trump administration, the newspaper claimed.
The report comes amid President Donald Trump’s push to eliminate what his administration calls “woke” ideology from the military and his longstanding clashes with mainstream media.
According to the Post, those hired include retired Air Force Colonel Rob Maness and retired Army Colonels Kurt Schlichter and Thomas Anderson. Some of their assignments could influence policy, the newspaper claims, citing anonymous sources familiar with the matter.
All three have reportedly received official civilian email accounts and been assigned to the office of Pentagon personnel chief Anthony Tata. His team has been tasked with addressing “culture-war issues,” including reviewing military colleges for “woke” ideology, according to the Post.
The newspaper goes on to cite a late August dispute involving conservative influencer Jennica Pounds as an example of the Pentagon’s social media efforts.
Pounds accused a State Department official of trying to “entrap” her into publishing government secrets as a journalistic scoop. US Undersecretary of State for Public Diplomacy Sarah Rogers later said she had approached Pounds and released the documents herself, prompting the influencer to apologize for “making a public spectacle” of the episode.
The Pentagon tightened press access rules last September as part of a broader crackdown on unauthorized disclosures following reports of turmoil inside the department. It has also reportedly considered using lie detector tests to identify officials leaking information.
Trump and Hegseth have repeatedly clashed with mainstream media over reports based on leaked documents and anonymous sources.
Earlier this month, Trump lashed out over reports that the war on Iran had significantly depleted US stocks of critical missiles and air defense interceptors, insisting no shortage existed.
“The ‘leakers’ of these treasonous statements are being hunted down. Long term jail sentences will be sought!” Trump wrote on Truth Social.

articles.title: The Defence Intelligence of Ukraine destroyed the Russian myth about "Tsirkon" – the missile turned out to be a solid-fuel ballistic missile
articles.body:
The Defence Intelligence of Ukraine destroyed the Russian myth about "Tsirkon" – the missile turned out to be a solid-fuel ballistic missile
Kyiv • UNN
The Defence Intelligence of Ukraine classified "Tsirkon" as a solid-fuel ballistic missile. Intelligence data refute the russian claims about a scramjet engine.
The Russian 3M22 "Tsirkon" missile, which Russia had presented for years as a unique hypersonic weapon with a ramjet engine, in fact turned out to be a solid-fuel ballistic missile. Defense Express reports this, citing data from the Main Intelligence Directorate of Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense, UNN writes.
Details
According to a report by Ukrainian intelligence, the "Tsirkon" does not have a hypersonic scramjet engine, as Russian propaganda had claimed for years.
After the booster completes its operation, the missile uses a 3L2211 solid-fuel rocket engine manufactured by Russia’s NPO Iskra. The Main Intelligence Directorate directly classifies the 3M22 "Tsirkon" as a ballistic missile.
It took about two years to determine the missile’s design
Defense Express notes that the Russian version of the "Tsirkon’s" design was considered plausible for a long time, even after Ukrainian specialists obtained fragments of the missile.
After analyzing the fragments in February 2024, the Kyiv Scientific Research Institute of Forensic Expertise stated that the missile had a jet engine rather than a solid-fuel engine. Some of the elements found had also previously been mistaken for fuel tanks characteristic of a different engine design.
The new data from the Main Intelligence Directorate, according to Defense Express, definitively refute Russia’s years-long claims about the supposedly high-tech scramjet hypersonic engine of the "Tsirkon" and change perceptions of the missile’s actual design.

articles.title: Ukraine’s War Chest Shrinks as Europe Mulls Gamble with Russia Billions
articles.body:
Europe’s grand €90 billion answer to Ukraine’s funding crisis survived for just eight months before Volodymyr Zelenskyy began proposing that part of next year’s allocation should be paid early.
Ukraine says it has already raided money earmarked for the second half of 2026 and is now staring down a €23.1 billion hole in its defense budget.

That is why a letter from the foreign ministers of Sweden, Poland, Spain and the Netherlands has dragged Europe’s Russian-frozen-assets fight back onto the table. The four governments say the €90 billion package will be insufficient and want Commission experts to explore new uses for Russia’s immobilized assets.
Bringing some of the 2027 money forward could fill part of this year’s hole. It would also obviously leave Ukraine with less money next year. That is the approaching financial cliff: Ukraine could run short again during 2027, while the EU’s next seven-year budget only begins in 2028. European governments would have to improvise another financial bridge in the meantime.
The letter therefore returns to the €210 billion in frozen Russian assets, presenting them as the rope that could pull Ukraine back from the financial cliff edge. What’s new in the letter is that it acknowledges that a way must be found to share the responsibility and liability of using the money, so that Belgium is not left carrying the risk alone, the obstacle that stalled the plan in December.
ISW Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment, August 30, 2026
Until now, the Russian principal has largely been reserved for Ukraine’s eventual reconstruction. Sikorski argues that “it is better to use it to stop the aggression … rather than wait until the end of Russia’s aggression to spend it on reconstruction”.
There is a clear logic here. Money spent defending Ukraine today can preserve its cities, factories and power stations, leaving less for Europe to rebuild later.
Next year is arriving early
Ukraine says its defense ministry faces a $27 billion, or €23.1 billion, funding gap this year. The shortfall includes around €6 billion in advance payments for equipment due in early 2027.
Zelenskyy has suggested advancing part of the EU money scheduled for 2027, although the Commission says it has yet to receive a formal request.
What is interesting here is that front-loading fits a pattern. If you look across Europe’s funding mechanisms, each one finds a different way to turn tomorrow’s resources into weapons or budget support today.
In simple terms, each plan reaches into a different part of the future. The G7 loan brings forward the profits that Russia’s assets will generate over many years. The €90 billion package places the EU budget behind money borrowed from financial markets while waiting for Russian reparations. The proposed reparations loan would use the underlying Russian cash, leaving Euroclear with an EU promise to replace it. That final step explains why collective guarantees are important as Europe may have to provide the money if it ever has to be returned to Moscow.
The instruments are distinct, and the same euro has not literally been spent several times. Even so, Europe has addressed successive immediate crises by placing claims on future profits, budgets and reparations.
There’s nothing crazy about it. Governments borrow all the time because urgent bills can’t always wait for tomorrow’s tax money. But clever financial tricks don’t make the political gamble vanish; they simply push the costs down the road. And sooner or later, someone will have to shoulder the risk if the promised reparations or government funds fail to cover the bill.
                                                                                                                                                                         
Belgium holds the vault and the risk
That responsibility leads to Belgium. Around €210 billion of Russian central-bank assets are immobilized in the EU, with roughly €185 billion held by Euroclear in Brussels.
Belgium slammed the brakes on the earlier reparations-loan plan, fearing a legal nightmare: Russian lawsuits, massive damages claims or a sudden order to hand the money back. The plan effectively asked Belgian to carry the risk for Europe’s geopolitical experiment, but Brussels insisted that any potential liability had to be shared across the continent.
The previous Commission proposal already went some way to recognizing that problem. It envisaged national guarantees divided according to each country’s share of EU gross national income, with coverage eventually moving to the EU budget.
The catch was that governments still had to sign up voluntarily, raising fears that chunks of the plan could be left without cover. Belgium demanded ironclad protection against every legal and financial threat so that it wouldn’t be stuck picking up the tab.
The letter puts the issue back on the table but stops well short of a deal. It offers no figure for the loan, no clear guarantee plan and no fix for Belgium’s objections. The four governments can force the issue back onto the agenda, but turning it into a workable plan will still require the backing of Europe’s biggest economies.
                                                                                                                                                                         
Survival comes before reconstruction
Poland’s Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski makes a strong case for taking the gamble. “Russia will not get this money back until it pays reparations to Ukraine, so it is better to use it to stop the aggression, that is, to defend Ukraine, rather than wait until the end of Russia’s aggression to spend it on reconstruction,” he said.
The logic is to spend the money now on air defenses, ammunition and Ukrainian weapons factories, and Ukraine may save its cities, power stations, factories and territory from destruction. Every building and piece of infrastructure left standing could mean a smaller reconstruction bill later. A stronger Ukraine could also have a better hand when peace talks eventually begin.
Of course, nobody can put an exact price tag on the calculation. One euro spent on defense will not automatically wipe a fixed amount off the reconstruction bill. Ukraine will still need vast sums after the war, while the frozen Russian assets are limited. But the order matters. There can be no meaningful reconstruction if Ukraine does not survive as a sovereign, functioning country.

articles.title: Former Ukrainian president has made offer to Zelenskyy amid Russia’s new type of war on Kyiv
articles.body:
Former Ukrainian President Petro Poroshenko, leader of the opposition European Solidarity party, has offered to unite with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in a new type of government. He has explained his initiative as necessary to save the country and adopt crisis-response measures amid a new phase of the war.
Russia's strike campaign has become a governance problem as much as a military one. Each attack on Kyiv costs the city about $12 million, and they now arrive almost twice a week. Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotskyi said on 28 August that, roughly speaking, 90% of retail chains' food logistics had been destroyed in the latest attacks, which included jet-powered drones that trigger an air alert in Kyiv every hour.
"We are the opposition, but we are ready to cooperate with the authorities in the legislative provision of all necessary decisions, up to the creation of a coalition and a government of national unity," he said.
Speaking in a video address on 31 August, he set out five issues to solve for the parliamentary session.
One: keep the capital running
The current barrage has forced Kyiv to a near-standstill, with alerts sounding through the working day. If they are permanent, Poroshenko argued, the rules for how the city runs must change, and the government, military, transport operators, and business must agree on a single published procedure. When the capital is shut down for hours, much of the economy stops with it, and the lost billions never reach the army, he added.
"Let us say honestly what Putin is doing. He wants to switch Kyiv off. To make people finally say: it is impossible to live here," Poroshenko said.
Two: give parents a school plan
The school year opens on 1 September under a rule allowing in-person classes only where a school has a shelter with room for everyone. Kyiv's administration told UNN that 94% of city schools have basic shelters, but capacity limits set the ceiling, forcing shifts or blended formats when a shelter cannot hold every child at once.
"Tomorrow is 1 September. Thousands of parents still do not understand how their children will study, especially where there are no proper shelters," Poroshenko said.
Three: return Kyiv's money
Kyiv has lost revenue to the central budget even as its defense costs climb, a dispute with the government that predates the barrage. Poroshenko demanded the return of about $180 million to the budget, along with the personal income tax paid by combat brigades.
"This week Kyiv is forced to carry out a budget sequester for the first time," he explained, cutting spending on doctors, teachers, and the socially vulnerable to fund the city's own defense.
Four: scale up war-risk insurance
Russia's strikes have hit businesses faster than any recovery system can answer, with warehouses and logistics hubs among the targets this month. Business needs war-risk insurance, money for rapid recovery after strikes, new logistics, and the ability to invest in its own protection, including private air defense, Poroshenko said.
Five: fund energy resilience now
Putin has named energy as his main target, the former president pointed out, and the coming winter is the pressure point. Kyiv's small, maneuverable generation, cogeneration, and backup power for hospitals, water utilities, and communications must be installed now, he added.

articles.title: Ukrainians turn anger on Kiev for storing explosives near their homes
articles.body:
Ukrainians turn anger on Kiev for storing explosives near their homes
Residents of the Kiev suburb of Milaya have accused Ukrainian officials of placing an ammunition depot dangerously close to civilian homes, according to interviews published by The Guardian on Monday.
The military storage site was hit last week during a Russian barrage. The Russian Defense Ministry said the attack targeted a warehouse complex storing components for Ukrainian long-range kamikaze drones used in strikes on logistics and e-commerce facilities in Russia.
Secondary explosions continued for hours after the strike, scattering stored military ordnance around homes just hundreds of meters from the depot, local residents told the British newspaper.
“Those who set up the depot here are to blame. There are people here, this is a village. You can’t keep something like that here,” Vera, 65, reportedly said.
She and her son Sergey spent hours sheltering in a small bunker beside their home as dozens of secondary explosions rocked the area.
“I thought it was humanitarian aid that was stored there,” Sergey told the newspaper.
The incident killed at least 38 people and damaged more than 200 private homes and 14 apartment buildings, the Kiev military administration said on Sunday. Thirty of those killed were residents of a care home located close to the ammunition depot, according to The Guardian.
Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky said an investigation had been launched into the “terrible negligence” that allowed munitions to be stored so close to civilians.
“Another such crime – after what happened in Vishnevoe – is absolutely unacceptable,” he wrote on X on Saturday.
A Russian strike on an ammunition depot in the Kiev suburb of Vishnevoe on July 6 also triggered massive secondary explosions, damaging hundreds of civilian buildings and causing civilian casualties. Following that incident, Zelensky and other senior Ukrainian officials vowed to prevent munitions from being stored near residential areas.
Storing ammunition near civilian housing could contravene international humanitarian law. Under Additional Protocol I to the Geneva Conventions, parties to a conflict must, “to the maximum extent feasible,” avoid locating military objectives within or near densely populated areas.

articles.title: Voorheis Takes Helm of Life Cycle Management Center with $400B Portfolio
articles.body:
Lt. Gen. Jason D. Voorheis has taken command of the Air Force Life Cycle Management Center, a sprawling organization with a $400 billion portfolio, establishing him as one of the service’s top acquisition officials.
Voorheis moves into the job having jumped the rank of major general. As a one star, he was program acquisition executive for command, control, communications, and battle management, or C3BM, the office overseeing the Air Force’s effort to create a massive “battle network.”
Voorheis assumed command of AFLCMC on Aug. 27 during a ceremony at the National Museum of the U.S. Air Force at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, Ohio, according to a release.
In his new role, Voorheis will also serve as the PAE for combat readiness and integrating PAE for mission systems.
AFLCMC has more than 21,000 employees and manages acquisition, upgrades, and support for aircraft, engines, munitions, electronics, and cyber systems. In other words, it’s the nerve center of keeping the service’s critical hardware running.
“Just about every aircraft, weapon system, uniform, and piece of gear our Airmen take into harm’s way is acquired, fielded, modernized, and sustained by the expertise within AFLCMC. You are the engine of our nation’s defense,” Voorheis told the center’s personnel at the ceremony.
Voorheis takes the post following the retirement of Lt. Gen. Donna D. Shipton, who also previously worked as the Integrating Program Executive Officer for Mission Systems.
Brig. Gen. Joshua Williams took over Voorheis’ previous role as the head of the C3BM office on Aug. 28, according to a separate release. The Air Force established C3BM in 2022, and Maj. Gen. Luke C.G. Cropsey served as its first commander, followed by Vorheis, who took over in February. Cropsey now serves as the military deputy to the Air Force acquisition executive in the Pentagon.
In bidding farewell to the C3BM office, Voorheis said his six months in the job included some of the “most rewarding experiences throughout my career.”
“The mission ahead does not pause,” Voorheis added. “Never stop challenging legacy processes that slow down capability delivery.”
The main goal of the C3BM office is to create a DAF Battle Network, an integrated system of systems that links sensor, effector, and logistics systems. With about 50 programs of record, it is the DAF’s piece of the Pentagon’s massive Combined Joint All Domain Command and Control effort, which seeks to connect any sensor, shooter, and logistics node to a shared network across all of the services.
But the three-star’s experience isn’t limited to the DAF Battle Network; he previously served as the program executive officer for fighters and advanced aircraft, the materiel leader for the F-15 program office, and system program director for the B-21 bomber, according to his official biography.
AFLCMC stood up in 2012 as part of an effort to consolidate and streamline operations within Air Force Materiel Command. It is one of six centers under AFMC, trimmed from a previous dozen centers the service operated, to lower costs, improve readiness, increase aircraft production, and reduce parts shortages, Air & Space Forces Magazine previously reported.
The other centers under AFMC are the Air Force Research Laboratory, the Air Force Nuclear Weapons Center, the Air Force Test Center, the Air Force Installation Management Center, and the Air Force Sustainment Center.

articles.title: Northrop gets $86M for security systems at nuclear missile bases
articles.body:
- The U.S. Air Force awarded Northrop Grumman an $86.1 million sole-source task order to maintain its Remote Visual Assessment missile silo monitoring system.
- Work covers four bases, Hill, F.E. Warren, Malmstrom and Minot, and is expected to run through September 2031.
The U.S. Air Force has awarded Northrop Grumman an $86.1 million task order to maintain the security cameras and sensors that watch over America’s nuclear missile silos.
The task order covers program management, maintenance, sustaining engineering and support services for the Remote Visual Assessment program, a ground-based camera and sensor network that monitors Minuteman III intercontinental ballistic missile silos. The award falls under a broader ground subsystem support contract Northrop Grumman has held since 2021. The Air Force Nuclear Weapons Center at Hill Air Force Base, Utah, is the contracting activity.
Work under this task order will take place at Hill Air Force Base, along with F.E. Warren Air Force Base in Wyoming, Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana, and Minot Air Force Base in North Dakota, the three installations that oversee the Air Force’s dispersed fields of Minuteman III silos across the northern United States. The contract is expected to run through September 2031.
The Remote Visual Assessment system lets Air Force personnel confirm what’s happening at a missile silo without physically traveling to the site, an important capability given how far apart individual silos sit across the missile fields. When a security sensor detects unusual activity at a silo, cameras tied into the RVA system let a missile alert facility crew visually verify the alert before dispatching a security response team, cutting down on unnecessary trips to remote locations.
The award was made as a sole-source acquisition, meaning the Air Force did not open the work to competitive bidding. Of the task order’s total value, $15.2 million in fiscal 2026 procurement funds was obligated at the time of award, with the remainder expected to be funded as the work progresses.

articles.title: Russia slams Japanese drills with US and Australia, says US Typhon missile systems pose threat
articles.body:
Russia slams Japanese drills with US and Australia, says US Typhon missile systems pose threat
VLADIVOSTOK, Russia, Sept 1 - Russia on Tuesday condemned upcoming joint military exercises between Japan, Australia and the United States and said it had formally complained to Tokyo about the deployment of U.S. Typhon missile launchers for the drills, something it said posed a threat to its own national security.
The "Orient Shield" drills are due to run from September 8-24 in Japan and, according to Japan's Kyodo News, will involve 3,700 personnel from the three countries, making the exercise the biggest of its kind yet. The drills will for the first time also involve U.S. Typhon mid-range missile systems which can launch SM-6 and Tomahawk cruise missiles.
Maria Zakharova, a spokeswoman for Russia's Foreign Ministry, told reporters at a news briefing in Vladivostok that Russia wanted Japan to return to a policy of pacifism and was concerned that the exercises would take place in Japanese regions close to Russia's own borders in the far east. Russia had lodged a complaint with the Japanese embassy in Moscow on Monday, she said.
"The Japanese side was firmly informed that provocative military activity near our country’s far eastern borders is categorically unacceptable,” said Zakharova.
"Attention was also drawn to reports that, as part of these exercises, it is intended to deploy American Typhon ground-based systems. It was made clear to the embassy that the deployment of such weapons on Japanese territory, including under the pretext of military exercises, is absolutely unacceptable as it poses a threat to Russia’s security. A warning was issued regarding compensatory countermeasures by Moscow aimed at ensuring an appropriate level of national security.”
The U.S. military sent its powerful Typhon midrange missile system to Kagoshima Prefecture for joint exercises with the Japanese Self-Defence Forces in June, the Japan Times reported at the time. It said the missiles were then scheduled to take part in this month's joint exercises before being moved to a U.S. military base in Japan from around mid-October.
Russia and Japan have exchanged a series of protests in recent weeks following a rare visit by President Vladimir Putin to a disputed Russian-controlled island off northeast Japan.
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi called the trip "absolutely unacceptable", and Moscow then summoned the Japanese ambassador to complain about what it called anti-Russian remarks by Takaichi and her foreign minister. REUTERS
